explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Jesus says "All the nations will be gathered before Him…" (Matthew 25:32). Not one group, not one city, ALL of them. That's a bigger crowd than my bakery on free cookie day, and I've never even had a free cookie day.

Good guess, friend, but the text doesn't say priests. Jesus says "All the nations will be gathered before Him…" (Matthew 25:32). The crowd is far wider than one group. It's a gathering with no VIP section.

Close to home, but the passage goes way bigger. Jesus says "All the nations will be gathered before Him…" (Matthew 25:32). That's every nation, not one city's leaders. Jerusalem's elders would need a MUCH bigger room.

Yes, the kingdom. The King says, "Come, you who are blessed by My Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you…" (Matthew 25:34). Notice the word inherit. An inheritance is something handed to you, not something you bake from scratch at midnight. I've tried that. The kitchen was NOT okay.

Land is a fair guess, since inheritances in the Bible often involve land. But the King says, "…inherit the kingdom prepared for you…" (Matthew 25:34). So it's a kingdom, friend, not a plot with a fence. Bigger gift, bigger bakery.
I see why you'd reach for temple, but that's not the word. The King says, "…inherit the kingdom prepared for you…" (Matthew 25:34). Kingdom is what He names. Keep that one in your apron pocket.

Not quite, friend. The King says the kingdom was prepared for them "from the foundation of the world" (Matthew 25:34). That's the opposite of last minute. It's been ready since the very beginning, which is more prep time than I've ever given a batch.

False is right. The King says the kingdom was "prepared for you from the foundation of the world" (Matthew 25:34). Nothing rushed about it. I'd have been sweating over that timer, but this was ready from the very start.

That's the one. The King says, "I was a stranger and you took Me in" (Matthew 25:35). Taking someone in means making room for them. I know how good that feels, because I was once a stranger in a drawer and somebody made room for me.
Directions are helpful, friend, I'll give you that. But the King says, "I was a stranger and you took Me in" (Matthew 25:35). Taking Him in is more than pointing down the road. It's opening the door.

explanations.answer: They sent Him on His way
explanations.explanation: Whoa, that's the opposite. The King says, "I was a stranger and you took Me in" (Matthew 25:35). Sending someone off is what the ones on the left will be told they did (Matthew 25:43). The ones on the right opened the door.
True. The King says, "I was in prison and you visited Me" (Matthew 25:36). It's the last thing on His list, after hungry, thirsty, stranger, naked and sick. Showing up counts, friend.
It's actually true. The King says, "I was in prison and you visited Me" (Matthew 25:36). That's the final item on His list of six. Don't let it slip past like a cookie off the cooling rack.

explanations.answer: When they ever saw Him that way
explanations.explanation: Right on. They ask, "Lord, when did we see You hungry and feed You…" (Matthew 25:37), and then they keep going down the list through the stranger, the naked and the sick and in prison (Matthew 25:38-39). I think they're honestly stunned. It's the same question six times, like me asking where I put my mustache wax. It's on my face. EVERY time.

explanations.answer: Why He never told them sooner
explanations.explanation: Nobody asks that, friend. The righteous ask, "Lord, when did we see You hungry and feed You…" (Matthew 25:37). Their question is about WHEN they saw Him, not why they weren't told. They're surprised, not complaining.

explanations.answer: How He made it through all that
explanations.explanation: That's a kind question, but it's not theirs. They ask, "Lord, when did we see You hungry and feed You…" (Matthew 25:37). They're asking when they ever saw Him in those spots. I think they had no idea.

That's it. The King replies, "Truly I tell you, whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me" (Matthew 25:40). What they did for them, He counts as done for Him. That answers their question right there.

The angels are there (Matthew 25:31), but the King doesn't mention anybody writing anything down. He says, "…whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me" (Matthew 25:40). His answer is about Him, friend, not a record book.

Double payment sounds nice, friend, but that's not what He says. The King replies, "…whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me" (Matthew 25:40). He says what they did for them, they did for Him. No coupon, no math.
That's right. The King says the eternal fire was "prepared for the devil and his angels" (Matthew 25:41). It's heavy stuff, friend, so I'll say it plain and leave it there.
That one's from a different story, friend. In this passage the King says the fire was "prepared for the devil and his angels" (Matthew 25:41). Baal's prophets don't show up here at all.

I see the jump, since all the nations are gathered here (Matthew 25:32). But the King names who it was prepared for: "the devil and his angels" (Matthew 25:41). It's a heavy line, so I'm going to keep it short.

Not quite, friend. The King's list is about what they DIDN'T do: "…you did not take Me in… you did not clothe Me… you did not look after Me" (Matthew 25:43). He doesn't say they were cruel. It's about what was left undone.

False is right. The King says, "I was a stranger and you did not take Me in, I was naked and you did not clothe Me, I was sick and in prison and you did not look after Me" (Matthew 25:43). It's what they didn't do, not cruel acts. This part is heavy, friend, and I think it's worth slowing down for.

True! They say, "Lord, when did we see You hungry or thirsty or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison, and did not minister to You?" (Matthew 25:44). It's the same kind of question the righteous asked (Matthew 25:37-39). Both groups were surprised, friend.

It's actually true. The ones on the left say, "Lord, when did we see You hungry or thirsty or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison, and did not minister to You?" (Matthew 25:44). The righteous asked a question too (Matthew 25:37-39). Both groups say they didn't see Him.

explanations.answer: They did not do it for Him
explanations.explanation: That's it. The King answers, "Truly I tell you, whatever you did not do for one of the least of these, you did not do for Me" (Matthew 25:45). It mirrors what He told the righteous (Matthew 25:40). Same King, same standard.

explanations.answer: Someone else should have done it
explanations.explanation: He doesn't say that, friend. The King answers, "…whatever you did not do for one of the least of these, you did not do for Me" (Matthew 25:45). He doesn't point at anyone else. His answer lands on Him.

explanations.answer: It was too small to count
explanations.explanation: Small things count with this King, friend. He says, "…whatever you did not do for one of the least of these, you did not do for Me" (Matthew 25:45). Nothing about it being too small. He takes it personally.
Yes, friend. Jesus ends with "…but the righteous into eternal life" (Matthew 25:46). That's where the story lands for them. It's a good ending to a heavy passage.
Going home sounds cozy, but that's not it. Jesus ends with "…but the righteous into eternal life" (Matthew 25:46). The destination is life that doesn't end.

Good thought, but the temple isn't in this picture at all. Jesus ends with "…but the righteous into eternal life" (Matthew 25:46). That's the last line, friend, and it's a hopeful one. The teaching on the Mount of Olives wraps up right there.
